turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Look, I've been out there nearly forty minutes and I'm wrecked. It's the right knee, can we just deal with that.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yep, sorry, this screen's decided to have a moment. Right knee, was it?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. Right one. It's been a niggle, nothing dramatic. Traffic on the freeway was a nightmare too, but anyway.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long's it been going on?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... three weeks? Maybe longer, I don't really know. I knelt on the bathroom tiles and it started after that.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? It just refreshed on me.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Right knee. After I knelt down. It's not that bad, just annoying when I'm on the stairs.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling? Or does it lock on you?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No swelling. It doesn't lock. Just aches going down stairs. I'm over it, honestly.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pain anywhere else? Your back?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Just the knee. And if you've got a second I need that council volunteering form signed, the one I dropped at the desk.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Form, right, hang on... I'm in the nurse's bit. Your blood pressure's come up high.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, yeah. White coat. I've been stuck in your waiting room, of course it's high.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): She's put one sixty-eight over ninety-six.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): There you go. It's always up in here and fine at home. Not that I check much.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a second one further down. One seventy-two over one hundred and two. Sorry, can you just hold while I... the cursor's jumped.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Both of them, fantastic. I feel fine. Can we not make a thing of it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any headaches, chest pain, funny vision?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I'm just knackered from work, that's all.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the knee, does it give way under you?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't give way. I already said it just aches.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, right. Are you on any tablets at the moment?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Panadol when it aches. Two of the five hundreds. Not every day.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, two of what? I was typing.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Two five-hundred milligram Panadol. Maybe three times a week, if that. I'm not religious about it.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else from the chemist, prescribed?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): No. My sister's mad on biotin, those gummies, reckons her hair's falling out. That's her problem, not mine.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Not yours. Any family history, heart or blood pressure?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Dad had a stroke. He ended up on perindopril after, I think. I'm not on that.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long ago was the stroke?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I dunno. Five-ish years? Maybe more. I wasn't keeping a diary.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. With those readings I was going to start you on a small dose of amlodipine today, five milligrams.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I don't want tablets. I told you it's the white coat. You're not starting me on something off two numbers from a nurse.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yeah, fair enough, let me rethink that. If it's white coat we shouldn't be starting a tablet off clinic readings alone.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you. Finally.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): So no new tablets today. Check it at home, morning and night, for a week. Chemist can lend a monitor, or I'll note a loan of the clinic one.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Morning and night for a week. Do I write them down or what? Parking meter's probably already gone, but go on.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Write them down, both numbers, with the time. Bring the sheet back.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): And the knee, while you're actually looking at me?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): From what you've said it sounds mechanical. Rest it, ice after the stairs, keep the Panadol as you are. If it locks or swells up, come back sooner.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): So no scan. Typical.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it's not settling in a fortnight we might do an x-ray. I'm not ordering one now.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): A fortnight. And you're still doing the form, yeah?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll sign the volunteering form once I've got those home readings, not today, because of the pressure. Come back in two weeks with the numbers.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. I've got work. Can it be an arvo, not crack of dawn?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Reception can book an afternoon. If any reading is over one-eighty systolic, or you get chest pain, don't sit on it, go to emergency.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, alright. Are we done? I need to get out of here.

procedures_and_investigations.name: knee x-ray
procedures_and_investigations.indication: if right knee pain is not settling in a fortnight

clinical_actions.description: Home blood pressure monitoring morning and night for a week

time_reference.value: if not settling in a fortnight

clinical_actions.description: Write down both blood pressure numbers with the time and bring the sheet back
Rest the knee, ice after stairs, and continue Panadol as currently taken
If a home reading is over 180 mmHg systolic or chest pain occurs, go to emergency

time_reference.value: if it locks or swells up

clinical_actions.description: Loan a clinic blood pressure monitor or arrange a chemist loan
Sign the volunteering form once home blood pressure readings are available

time_reference.value: if it locks or swells up

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient cannot date the start of the right knee pain more precisely than about three weeks and said it may have been longer.
The patient cannot date the father's stroke more precisely than about five years.

ambiguous_entities: Two different clinic blood pressure readings were read aloud (168/96 and 172/102) and no single representative value was chosen.
The patient said home blood pressure is fine but also said they do not check it much.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
